newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's raises minimum wage by 21.02 pct.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's raises minimum wage by 21.02 pct.

text.p: President Ernesto Samper issued a decree Monday raising Colombia's minimum wage 21.02 percent from January 1.
The wage rise will directly benefit about four million workers now earning the legal minimum and will take their monthly pay to 172,005 pesos (about $172) from 142,125 pesos.

But the rise has found little favor with the country's largest union federations, which initially pushed for a 27 percent increase and, after extensive negotiations, said they would settle for one percentage point above inflation.

The year-end inflation figure is scheduled for release Thursday and is expected to be higher than the 21.02 percent increase in the minimum wage. Inflation in the 11 months to November was running at 20.76 percent, well above the 17 percent annual target the government set at the start of 1996.

Samper was forced to raise the minimum wage by decree after wage-price negotiations, known as the Social Pact, between the government, employers and workers' representatives broke down just before Christmas.

The three main unions, the Communist-led Single Workers' Confederation, the Christian Democrat-led General Confederation of Democratic Workers and the Liberal-dominated Colombian Workers' Confederation, argue a worker needs at least two-and-a-half minimum wages to live decently and that the Social Pact has suppressed wages, but failed to peg inflation, eroding salaries in real terms. They are threatening a program of strikes and stoppages for 1997.
